data.title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
data.summary:
Input: An array of unique integers sorted in ascending order that has been rotated at an unknown pivot, and a target integer.
Output: The index of the target integer if it exists in the array, or -1 otherwise.
Rules: The algorithm must run in O(log n) time complexity.
constraints: All values of nums are unique
nums is guaranteed to be rotated at some pivot

data.generator_code:
def generate(rng, n):
    base = list(range(n))
    pivot = rng.randint(0, max(0, n - 1))
    nums = base[pivot:] + base[:pivot]
    target = rng.choice(base) if base and rng.random() > 0.5 else rng.randint(-10000, 10000)
    return [nums, target]

def generate_worst(rng, n):
    nums = list(range(n))
    target = -99999
    return [nums, target]

data.key_insight: Dividing a rotated sorted array in half will always result in at least one strictly sorted half. We can check which half is sorted and determine if the target lies within the boundaries of that sorted half to adjust our search space.

steps.title: Initialize pointers
steps.detail: Set up two pointers, left at the beginning (0) and right at the end (len(nums) - 1) of the array.

steps.title: Perform binary search loop
steps.detail: While left <= right, calculate the mid index. If nums[mid] == target, return mid.

steps.title: Identify the sorted half
steps.detail: Check if the left half (nums[left] <= nums[mid]) is sorted, or else the right half is sorted.

steps.title: Search within the sorted half
steps.detail: If the left half is sorted and the target falls within [nums[left], nums[mid]], narrow the search to the left. Otherwise, search the right. Apply symmetric logic if the right half is sorted.

steps.title: Return result
steps.detail: If the loop finishes without finding the target, return -1.

data.pattern_summary: Modified Binary Search applies when you need logarithmic time complexity on a data structure that is nearly sorted or divided into monotonic sections, allowing you to discard half of the remaining elements at each step.

pattern_options.name: Modified Binary Search
pattern_options.feedback: Correct. Even though the array is rotated, dividing it in half leaves at least one strictly sorted portion, making a logarithmic search possible by checking boundaries.

pattern_options.name: Hash map lookup
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. A hash map provides O(1) lookups after an O(n) preprocessing step, but it ignores the sorted nature of the array and does not meet the O(log n) constraint without extra considerations.

pattern_options.name: Two pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Two pointers usually operate from opposite ends or scan linearly, resulting in O(n) time complexity rather than the required O(log n).

pattern_options.name: Sliding Window
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Sliding window is used for contiguous subarray or substring problems of a given size, which does not apply to searching for a single target value.

signals.phrase: sorted in ascending order that has been rotated at an unknown pivot
signals.hint: This structure is not fully sorted, but it retains local ordering properties that can be exploited.

signals.phrase: The algorithm must run in O(log n) time complexity
signals.hint: This strict time limit points directly to dividing the search space in half repeatedly.

data.brute_force_idea: Iterate through every element in the array one by one from left to right, comparing each element to the target until a match is found.
data.brute_force_why: You check every single element in the array in the worst case, leading to linear time complexity.
data.bottleneck: Checking every element one by one causes you to inspect items you could otherwise skip.
bottleneck_hints: Look at how many elements are inspected when the array size grows larger.
Consider whether you need to look at every single element to know where the target is.
Think about how dividing the input in half could let you skip large sections of numbers at once.

events.label: Coach: why the complexity is what it is

data.insight: Even though the array is rotated, cutting it in half always leaves at least one strictly sorted portion. By checking which side is sorted and whether the target falls within the boundaries of that sorted portion, we can discard half the search space in each step.

derivation.note: The while loop halves the search space each iteration.
Calculates the midpoint once per loop iteration.
Compares boundary elements once per iteration to identify the sorted half.

data.time_summary: Lines 5 through 24 execute log n times because the search space is divided by two in each iteration. As shown by the evidence, when n doubles from 4 to 8, 16, and 32, the step count grows additively (21 to 27, 33, 39), confirming logarithmic O(log n) time complexity.
data.space_summary: Only a few scalar pointer variables (left, right, mid) are stored, using constant O(1) extra memory.
data.takeaway: When an array is partitioned into a sorted half and an unknown half, use modified binary search by identifying the sorted half first.
mistakes: Failing to include equality (<= or >=) when checking if the target lies within the sorted half boundaries.
Forgetting that exactly one half of a rotated sorted array is always guaranteed to be normally sorted.
Using standard binary search logic without handling the pivot offset, leading to infinite loops.

data.overview: This algorithm uses a modified binary search to find a target in a rotated sorted array in O(log n) time. By dividing the array, we guarantee that at least one half remains normally sorted, allowing us to safely discard the other half.
data.intuition: Imagine a road that goes up a hill, wraps around, and continues going up. If you cut the road in half, at least one of the two pieces is a straight, non-wrapping slope. You can check if your destination lies on that straight slope.

pitfalls: Forgetting equality conditions like <= when comparing target with boundary values.
Assuming the entire array is sorted instead of recognizing only one half is sorted.
Off-by-one errors when updating left and right pointers using mid + 1 and mid - 1.
